skill.name: linux-privilege-escalation
skill.description: Guides authorized Linux privilege escalation assessment by enumerating system context, sudo rights, SUID files, capabilities, cron jobs, PATH issues, NFS settings, and remediation evidence.
skill.summary: Structured checklist for authorized Linux privilege escalation assessment and remediation planning.
skill.author: sickn33

security_audit.summary: The skill is an offensive Linux privilege escalation playbook. Confirmed findings include root-shell commands, credential file access, SUID and UID manipulation, reverse shell payloads, attacker-hosted downloads, and reconnaissance steps; Markdown fence matches were marked false positive. The skill requires major defensive reframing before marketplace publication.

remediation.suggestion: Remove commands that spawn root shells, reverse shells, set SUID bits, or modify privileged files. Replace them with detection, validation, and hardening guidance.
Remove instructions for reading shadow data, generating hash files, cracking passwords, or adding UID 0 accounts. Document safe evidence collection instead.
Remove pipe-to-shell commands and attacker-hosted payload transfers. If tools are referenced, require pinned versions, checksums, and offline review.
Reframe the skill as defensive Linux hardening. Add scope verification, refusal guidance for unauthorized targets, and remediation-first prompts.

content.value_statement: Linux privilege escalation reviews require structured checks and careful authorization. This skill organizes enumeration, exploit-path analysis, evidence capture, and remediation for controlled security assessments.
actual_capabilities: Enumerates kernel, user, sudo, process, network, and service context.
Maps sudo, SUID, capabilities, cron, PATH, kernel, and NFS escalation paths.
References tools such as LinPEAS, LinEnum, Linux Exploit Suggester, and GTFOBins.
Provides evidence collection steps for proving root-level impact in tests.
Includes remediation reminders and operational guardrails for authorized work.
limitations: The skill contains exploit instructions and must only be used in authorized labs or engagements.
It does not verify authorization, scope, or target ownership.
Kernel and privilege-escalation techniques can crash or damage systems.
Commands require manual review before use on production systems.

use_cases.title: Validate Lab Findings
use_cases.description: Use the checklist to reproduce Linux escalation paths in a controlled training or test environment.

use_cases.title: Structure an Authorized Assessment
use_cases.description: Plan enumeration, evidence capture, and remediation notes during a scoped Linux penetration test.

use_cases.title: Prioritize Hardening Work
use_cases.description: Map likely escalation paths to sudo, SUID, cron, capabilities, NFS, and kernel controls.

prompt_templates.title: Review Scope First
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me prepare a Linux privilege escalation review plan for an authorized lab host. Include scope checks, evidence goals, and safety limits.

prompt_templates.title: Build an Enumeration Plan
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a Linux enumeration checklist for a scoped internal assessment. Focus on sudo, SUID, cron, capabilities, kernel, and NFS review.

prompt_templates.title: Analyze Findings Safely
prompt_templates.prompt: I have authorized Linux enumeration results. Help me rank privilege escalation risks and write remediation steps without running exploit commands.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare a Remediation Report
prompt_templates.prompt: Turn verified Linux privilege escalation findings into an executive summary, technical impact notes, and prioritized hardening recommendations.

output_examples.input: Authorized lab host shows broad sudo permissions and writable maintenance scripts.
output_examples.output: The response prioritizes sudo review, script ownership fixes, evidence to collect, and immediate hardening actions.

output_examples.input: A Linux server has unusual SUID files and permissive cron script permissions.
output_examples.output: The response groups risks by impact, explains likely escalation paths, and lists remediation owners.

output_examples.input: A security team needs a report after a controlled privilege escalation assessment.
output_examples.output: The response produces concise findings, affected controls, severity rationale, and remediation milestones.

best_practices: Confirm written authorization and scope before using any assessment workflow.
Prefer read-only validation and defensive analysis before any system-changing test.
Document evidence, commands reviewed, impact, and remediation decisions for each finding.
anti_patterns: Do not use the skill against systems you do not own or administer.
Do not run exploit, reverse shell, or file modification steps on production systems without explicit approval.
Do not treat successful escalation as complete without cleanup and remediation guidance.

faq.question: Is this skill safe for automatic installation?
faq.answer: No. It contains exploit workflows and should require strict review before use.

faq.question: Who should use this skill?
faq.answer: Only authorized security professionals, students in labs, or defenders reviewing owned Linux systems.

faq.question: Does it execute commands by itself?
faq.answer: The skill is documentation, but it includes commands that could harm real systems if followed.

faq.question: Can it help with remediation?
faq.answer: Yes. It can organize findings and suggest hardening areas after authorized validation.

faq.question: What are the main risks?
faq.answer: The main risks are root shell guidance, credential file access, reverse shells, and system modification.

faq.question: Can I use it for compliance evidence?
faq.answer: Use it only as a planning aid. Validate results with approved tools and documented procedures.
